01.note: Rabbi Elazar went into a bathroom, and a Roman came and pushed him out. Rabbi Elazar got up and left. A serpent then came and ripped out the Roman's intestines. Rabbi Elazar applied a verse to him, "Therefore I will give man for you," reading the Hebrew word for "man" (adam) as "Edom," a name the Sages used for Rome.
01.why: The Gemara is gathering teachings and incidents about conduct and modesty in the bathroom; this one follows the story of Rav Safra and Rabbi Abba at a bathroom door, and is followed by a lesson drawn from Saul's modesty in the cave.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who was pushed out of a bathroom by a Roman, and who applied a verse to the Roman's death.

terms.meaning: The nation descended from Esau. The Sages used the name as a code word for Rome, which is why Rabbi Elazar rereads "adam" (man) as "Edom" (a Roman).

02.note: Rav Safra reports a story Rabbi Abbahu used to tell. Hanina, nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, went to Babylonia and began fixing the calendar there, a task reserved for the Land of Israel. The Sages of Israel sent two scholars after him. At first he praised them publicly, but when they kept overturning his rulings he called them worthless; they answered that he could not tear down what he had built up. Their reason: he was fixing the calendar outside the Land. He cited Rabbi Akiva's example and his own stature, but they replied that the young students he left behind had grown into horned goats, and that he must obey or be ostracized. If the Babylonian Jews refused, they should declare they had no portion in the God of Israel. The whole people burst into tears and said they did.
02.why: Right after the story the Gemara asks why the Sages of Israel went to such lengths, and answers with the verse "For out of Zion shall go forth the Torah"; it then asks how the visitors were allowed to overturn another Sage's rulings.

people.name: Hanina
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehoshua's brother; he went to Babylonia and fixed the calendar there.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage who used to tell this story, as Rav Safra reports.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: The Sage who passes on Rabbi Abbahu's account.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Keifar
people.about: One of the two scholars the Sages of Israel sent after Hanina.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: An earlier Sage whom Hanina cites as having also fixed the calendar outside the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: Fixing the Jewish calendar: deciding when a new month begins and when to add a leap month to a year. The law reserves this authority for the Land of Israel.
Placed under a ban by the Sages, so that the community keeps its distance from the person until he submits.
The Jewish communities living outside the Land of Israel; here, Babylonia.

03.note: Rav Yosef was called "Sinai" for his vast knowledge, and Rabba "one who uproots mountains" for his sharpness. When one of them had to be chosen to head the yeshiva, they asked the Sages of the Land of Israel which came first, and were told "Sinai," since everyone needs the owner of the wheat. Rav Yosef still declined, because Chaldean astrologers had told him he would preside for only two years. Rabba presided for twenty-two years and then Rav Yosef for two and a half. All the years Rabba led, Rav Yosef did not even summon a bloodletter to his home.
03.why: Rabbi Avin HaLevi has just taught that one who yields to the moment finds the moment yields to him; the Gemara brings Rav Yosef, who gave up the post and still received it later, as the proof.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Called "Sinai" for his erudition; offered the headship of the yeshiva, he declined it.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Called "one who uproots mountains" for his sharpness; he headed the yeshiva for twenty-two years.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study; its head was the leading authority of the community of scholars.
Stargazers from Babylonia whose predictions were widely consulted; here they foretold the length of Rav Yosef's tenure.
A practitioner who drew blood as a medical treatment. Rav Yosef went to the bloodletter rather than having him come to his home, so as not to act like a man in authority.

04.note: Rav Hisda was holding two of the priestly gifts from an ox and announced he would give them to anyone who told him a new teaching of Rav. Rava bar Mehasseya told him Rav's teaching that one who gives a gift must let the recipient know, and Rav Hisda gave him the gifts. Rava bar Mehasseya asked whether Rav's teachings were really so dear to him, and Rav Hisda said yes. Rava bar Mehasseya then quoted another saying of Rav: fine wool is precious to those who wear it. Rav Hisda said he liked this second saying even more, and had he held another gift he would have given that too.
04.why: The Gemara has just cited, through Rava bar Mehasseya, Rav's ruling that a giver must inform the recipient, and worked through an objection to it; this story shows Rava bar Mehasseya first telling that ruling to Rav Hisda.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who offered priestly gifts to anyone who brought him a new teaching of Rav.

people.name: Rava bar Mehasseya
people.about: The Sage who told Rav Hisda two teachings of Rav and received the gifts.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The earlier Sage whose teachings Rav Hisda cherished.

terms.term: gifts of the priesthood from an ox
terms.meaning: Portions of a slaughtered animal that the Torah assigns to a priest. Here Rav Hisda, who held them, offered them as a reward for a new teaching.

05.note: Rav Yehoshua son of Rav Idi visited the house of Rav Ashi, and they prepared a choice calf for him and asked him to eat. He said he was fasting. They asked whether he did not accept Rav Yehuda's ruling that a person may postpone a fast and make it up another day. He answered that it was a fast for a dream, and quoted the teachings that a fast works against a bad dream like fire on chaff, that it must be on the same day, and that it is allowed even on Shabbat.
05.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav's teaching that fasting counters a bad dream, with Rav Hisda's and Rav Yosef's additions; the story shows a Sage relying on exactly those teachings to refuse a meal.

people.name: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: A visitor at Rav Ashi's house who declined the meal because he was fasting over a dream.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The host at whose house a calf was prepared for the guest.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose ruling that a fast can be borrowed and repaid later is quoted to the guest.

terms.meaning: A calf whose meat was considered especially fine; preparing one was a mark of honor for a guest.
A fast undertaken after a frightening dream, believed to cancel its bad omen. Unlike other fasts it cannot be postponed to another day.

06.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha said he could read by lamplight on Shabbat without tilting the lamp to adjust the wick. Once he read and found himself about to tilt it, and he said, how great are the words of the Sages who forbade reading by lamplight. Rabbi Natan tells it differently: he read and actually tilted it, then wrote in his notebook, "I, Yishmael ben Elisha, read and tilted a lamp on Shabbat; when the Temple is rebuilt I will bring a fat sin-offering."
06.why: Rava has ruled that an important person may read by lamplight because he would not handle a lamp; the Gemara objects with this story, and Rabbi Abba answers that Rabbi Yishmael was different, since in Torah study he behaved like an ordinary man.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: A Sage who claimed he could read by lamplight on Shabbat without adjusting the wick, and either nearly did or did.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who gives a different account of what Rabbi Yishmael did.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that an important person may read by lamplight on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Explains why Rabbi Yishmael's case does not refute Rava.

terms.meaning: Tilting an oil lamp so the oil reaches the wick and burns brighter. On Shabbat this counts as kindling, which is forbidden, so the Sages barred reading by lamplight in case one does it absent-mindedly.
An animal sacrifice brought in the Temple to atone for breaking a law by mistake.
A collection of early rabbinic teachings from the same era as the Mishna, often quoted in the Gemara.

07.note: A student who had studied much Mishna and Bible and served Torah scholars died at half his days. His widow carried his phylacteries around the synagogues and study halls, asking how the Torah could promise long life to its students when her husband died young, and no one answered her. Eliyahu tells that he stayed at her house and asked how her husband behaved during her menstrual period. She said he never touched her even with his little finger, but in the clean days that followed, while she was still counting, he ate and drank with her and slept beside her with bodily contact, without thinking of relations. Eliyahu said, blessed is the Omnipresent who killed him, for he showed no regard for the Torah. Later Sages said they shared one bed without contact, or with a garment between them.
07.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that a man may not lie even fully clothed beside his wife while she is menstruating, against Rabbi Pedat's view that only actual relations are forbidden; this teaching of the school of Eliyahu supports the stricter view.

people.name: Eliyahu
people.about: The narrator of the account, who stayed with the widow and gave her the explanation for her husband's death.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and said the couple slept in one bed without contact.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage quoted in the Land of Israel as saying a garment separated the husband and wife.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn on the arm and head during weekday morning prayer. The widow carried her husband's as a sign of his piety.
After a menstrual period ends, a woman counts seven clean days, checking with white cloths, before immersing. Until then the prohibition on her husband still applies.
A collection of teachings attributed to the prophet Elijah, who in rabbinic tradition visits and teaches the Sages.

08.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name: Hananya ben Hizkiya is remembered for good, because without him the book of Ezekiel would have been suppressed, since parts of it contradict the Torah. Three hundred jugs of oil were brought up to him, and he sat in his upper room and interpreted the book until the contradictions were resolved.
08.why: The mishna has named the upper room of Hananya ben Hizkiya ben Garon, where the Sages issued eighteen decrees, and the Gemara has just credited him and his circle with writing Megillat Taanit; this is a second thing he is remembered for.

people.name: Hananya ben Hizkiya
people.about: A Sage who, shut away in his upper room, reconciled the book of Ezekiel with the Torah.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports this teaching in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The earlier Sage whose praise of Hananya ben Hizkiya Rav Yehuda passes on.

terms.meaning: Withdrawn from public use and kept out of the books read as Scripture. The Sages considered doing this to Ezekiel because some of its laws seemed to contradict the Torah.
A room on the roof of a house, often used for study and meetings of the Sages.

09.note: In a dispute over whether grapes picked for the press can become ritually impure, Hillel challenged Shammai, and Shammai answered that if Hillel provoked him he would decree impurity on olive picking as well. A sword was planted in the study hall: whoever wished could come in, but no one could leave. That day Hillel sat bowed before Shammai like one of the students, and the day was as hard for Israel as the day the Golden Calf was made. Shammai and Hillel issued the decree and the people did not accept it; their students later issued it, and the people accepted it.
09.why: The Gemara is counting the eighteen decrees issued on one day when Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel; the decree on grapes picked for the press is one of them, and the story describes that day. Afterward the Gemara asks for the reason behind this decree.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: A leading Sage who threatened to extend his ruling on grape picking to olives.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A leading Sage, Shammai's opponent, who that day sat before Shammai like a student.

terms.meaning: In the laws of ritual purity, food can only become impure after it has been wet by certain liquids. The question is whether juice seeping from grapes makes them susceptible.
The idol the Israelites made in the wilderness, the Torah's byword for a national disaster.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and to decide the law.

10.note: Abaye gave a dyed garment to a launderer and asked what he would charge. The launderer asked the same price as for a white garment. Abaye told him the Sages had already anticipated him. Abaye also advised that anyone giving clothes to a launderer should measure them when handing them over and when taking them back: if longer, he has stretched and spoiled them; if shorter, he has shrunk them.
10.why: The Gemara has just inferred from Rabban Gamliel's household custom that white garments are harder to launder than colored ones; Abaye uses that very teaching to refuse the launderer's price.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who refused to pay a launderer the white-garment price for a dyed garment.

11.note: A student in the town of Harta De'argiz issued a ruling that followed Rabbi Shimon, and Rav Hamnuna excommunicated him. The Gemara asks why, since the law does follow Rabbi Shimon, and answers that the town was Rav's place, so the student should not have ruled against Rav there. The Gemara then mentions two students rescuing belongings from a fire on Shabbat: one carried a single vessel at a time, the other four or five at once.
11.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute between Rav, who forbids using set-aside items on Shabbat, and Shmuel, who permits them, matching an earlier dispute of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon; the student's ruling was on that question, given in the town where Rav's ruling held.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who excommunicated a student for ruling in Rav's town against Rav's view.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: An earlier Sage whose lenient view the student followed.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose town it was, and whose stricter view the student's ruling went against.

terms.meaning: Placed under a ban by a Sage, so that the community keeps its distance from the person until he submits.
A town under a particular Sage's authority. Even where the law is lenient, a student may not publicly rule against the local master there; it is an act of disrespect.

11.flag: The story segment joins the excommunicated student with an unrelated brief mention of two students rescuing vessels from a fire, which has no plot of its own.

12.note: Ravin and Abaye were walking in the valley of Tamrurita and saw some willow trees. Ravin told Abaye that this was the idan the mishna speaks of. Abaye objected that it was just wood. Ravin peeled off the bark and showed him the wool-like fibers between the bark and the trunk.
12.why: The Gemara is going through the mishna's list of materials that may not be used as wicks for the Shabbat lamp, identifying each one; just before, Ravin and Abaye identified another item on the list.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who identified the willow as the mishna's idan and proved it by peeling the bark.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Ravin's companion on the walk, who doubted that wood could make a wick.

terms.meaning: One of the materials the mishna forbids as a wick for the Shabbat lamp because it does not burn well; the Gemara identifies it as willow fiber.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara comments on line by line.

13.note: The Sages taught that the eight days of Hanukkah begin on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, and that no one may eulogize or fast on them. When the Greeks entered the Sanctuary, they defiled all its oils. When the Hasmonean dynasty overpowered and defeated them, they searched and found only one cruse of oil still bearing the High Priest's seal, with enough to light the candelabrum for a single day. A miracle happened and they lit from it for eight days. The following year these days were fixed as festive days of praise and thanksgiving.
13.why: The Gemara has been laying out how the Hanukkah lights are kindled, where the lamp is placed and when another light is needed; it then stops to ask what Hanukkah is, and this account is its answer.

terms.meaning: An ancient list of days of deliverance on which fasting and eulogies were forbidden; the Gemara quotes its entry for Hanukkah.
The priestly family, known also as the Maccabees, who led the revolt against the Greek rulers and then ruled Judea.
The inner hall of the Temple in Jerusalem, where the candelabrum (menorah) stood and was lit each day with pure olive oil.
A set of joyful psalms of praise recited on festivals.

14.note: Rav Huna taught that one who is regular about lighting lamps will have sons who are Torah scholars. Rav Huna used to pass by the door of Rabbi Avin the carpenter and saw that he lit many lamps; he said two great men would come from that house, and Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Hiyya bar Avin came from it. Rav Hisda likewise passed by the family home of Rav Sheizvi, saw many lamps lit there, and said a great man would come from it; Rav Sheizvi did.
14.why: The Gemara has just set the order of priority among the Shabbat lamp, the Hanukkah lamp and the wine for kiddush; Rav Huna's teaching on the reward for lighting lamps, and the two cases that bear it out, follow from that discussion.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who taught that lighting lamps earns sons who are scholars, and foresaw great men from Rabbi Avin's house.

people.name: Rabbi Avin the carpenter
people.about: A man who lit many lamps; his sons became the Sages Rav Idi and Rav Hiyya.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Son of Rabbi Avin the carpenter, one of the two great men Rav Huna foresaw.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who foresaw that a great man would come from Rav Sheizvi's family home.

people.name: Rav Sheizvi
people.about: The great man who came from the household where Rav Hisda saw many lamps lit.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with Torah verses fixed to a doorpost.
Tzitzit: knotted threads the Torah requires on the corners of a four-cornered garment.
The blessing over wine that proclaims the holiness of Shabbat or a festival.

15.note: A mother-in-law who hated her daughter-in-law told her to go and adorn herself with balsam oil. She did. When she came back, the mother-in-law told her to go and light the lamp. She went and lit it, and she caught fire and was burned.
15.why: The Gemara is discussing why balsam sap may not be used to light the Shabbat lamp, and Abaye has given the reason that it is volatile and dangerous; the story shows how deadly that volatility can be.

terms.meaning: A fragrant oil made from the sap of the balsam tree, prized as a perfume. The Gemara treats it as highly flammable, so a woman anointed with it was in danger near an open flame.

16.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalled a Shabbat he spent in the upper room of the house of Nit'za in Lod. They were brought an eggshell, filled it with oil, pierced it and set it over the lamp so it would keep feeding the flame. Rabbi Tarfon and other Elders were there and said nothing to them. The Rabbis answered him that this proves nothing: the people of the house of Nit'za were vigilant.
16.why: The mishna records a dispute: the Rabbis forbid setting a pierced, oil-filled eggshell over a lamp on Shabbat, in case one takes oil from it; Rabbi Yehuda permits it and offers this Shabbat as proof. Afterward a Sage warns that the Elders' silence led to a mistaken leniency.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who permits the eggshell device and recalls using it in the house of Nit'za.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: One of the Elders present that Shabbat, who said nothing about the eggshell.

terms.meaning: The majority of Sages in a dispute, as opposed to the individual Sage who disagrees with them.
A room on the roof of a house, often used by the Sages for study and gatherings.
Senior Sages.

17.note: A man came before Rabbi and told him, "Your wife is my wife and your children are my children." Rabbi asked whether he would like a cup of wine; the man drank and burst. Another man came before Rabbi Hiyya and said, "Your mother is my wife and you are my son." Rabbi Hiyya offered him a cup of wine too, and he drank and burst. Rabbi Hiyya said Rabbi's prayer had protected him from having his children branded mamzerim, for after praying Rabbi used to ask God to save him that day from impudent people and from insolence.
17.why: The Gemara has just resolved two verses of Proverbs, one saying to answer a fool and one saying not to, by ruling that a fool is not answered on worldly matters; these two Sages, insulted personally, gave their accusers no reply.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, called simply Rabbi; a man claimed his wife and children as his own.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whom a man claimed as his son; he explains how Rabbi's prayer protected him.

terms.meaning: Children born of a forbidden union, such as adultery. In Jewish law they are barred from marrying most other Jews, so the charge was a grave slander on Rabbi's children.

18.note: Rabban Gamliel was teaching that in the future a woman will give birth every day, citing the verse "The woman with child and her that gives birth together." A student scoffed, quoting "There is nothing new under the sun." Rabban Gamliel said, "Come and I will show you an example of this in this world," took him outside, and showed him a hen.
18.why: The Gemara has resolved two verses of Proverbs by ruling that a fool is answered when he challenges the Torah, though not on worldly matters; Rabban Gamliel answering the scoffing student is its example of the first kind, followed by two more like it.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage teaching about the world to come who answered a scoffing student with a hen.

terms.meaning: Drew a teaching from a verse by reading it closely and creatively, beyond its plain sense.
The perfected world of the future that the Sages describe, in contrast to this world.

19.note: Rabban Gamliel taught that in the future trees will bear fruit every day, reading the verse "And it shall bring forth branches and bear fruit" to mean that just as a branch grows every day, so will fruit. The same student scoffed, "Isn't it written, there is nothing new under the sun?" Rabban Gamliel said he would show him an example in this world, went outside, and showed him a caper bush.
19.why: This is the second of three cases the Gemara gives for its ruling that a fool who challenges the Torah should be answered; it follows Rabban Gamliel's reply with the hen.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage teaching about the world to come who answered a scoffing student with a caper bush.

terms.meaning: A shrub with edible buds and fruit; some part of it can be eaten in every season, so it seems to bear produce all year.
The perfected world of the future that the Sages describe, in contrast to this world.

20.note: Rabban Gamliel taught that in the future the Land of Israel will bring forth ready-made cakes and fine woolen garments, citing "Let abundant grain be in the land." Once again the student scoffed that there is nothing new under the sun. Rabban Gamliel went outside and showed him truffles and mushrooms for the cakes, and for the woolen garments, the fibrous covering of a young palm branch.
20.why: This is the third of the cases the Gemara gives for its ruling that a fool who challenges the Torah should be answered; the Gemara then turns to Hillel's patience under provocation.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage teaching about the world to come who answered a scoffing student with mushrooms and palm fiber.

terms.meaning: Fungi that spring up from the ground overnight, here offered as a small-scale example of bread-like food growing from the earth.
The tender new growth at the top of a palm tree, wrapped in a thin, net-like covering that looks like woven cloth.
